# IELTS Writing Task 1 General Training — complete guide synthesis

**Source:** IELTS Advantage, [IELTS Writing Task 1 General Training: Complete Guide](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aWgl7Wlw614), approximately 1 h 1 m.  
**Transcript:** complete auto-generated English captions exported and reviewed (884 lines). The video teaches a formal/informal contrast, then includes a student planning and writing an informal letter and a second student revising a formal letter. It overlaps with the shorter [2026 formal-letter demonstration](writing-task1-general-formal-letter-2026.md).

## Chapter map reconstructed from the transcript

- 0:00–2:58 — Task format; intended recipient; source’s formal/informal rule
- 2:58–10:49 — Formal letter structure and worked airline complaint
- 10:49–20:43 — Informal register and transformation of the airline story
- 20:43–43:19 — Student plans and drafts an informal reunion letter; feedback and review
- 43:19–1:00:35 — Student plans and revises a formal moving-company letter

## 1. Correctly identify purpose and register

The prompt gives a situation, a recipient, three bullet points, and sometimes the required opening. Read the full task before planning. Identify what the reader needs to understand or do, then respond to each bullet point.

The video teaches that a letter to a friend is informal and every other letter is formal. **This is not a complete IELTS rule.** IELTS General Training letters may be personal, semi-formal, or formal. A manager, teacher, landlord, or colleague may call for a semi-formal register depending on the relationship and context. Choose the register from the whole situation and maintain it consistently; do not force every prompt into a friend/not-friend binary. ([IELTS General Training Writing format](https://ielts.org/take-a-test/test-types/ielts-general-training-test/ielts-general-training-format-writing); [IELTS Writing preparation resources](https://ielts.org/take-a-test/preparation-resources/writing-test-resources))

The source claims that no semi-formal category exists. That claim is wrong. As a result, its informal/formal examples are useful contrasts, but its test-day classification shortcut should not be copied into a course rule.

## 2. A practical plan for any letter — 2:58–5:24; 21:00–25:57

The instructor’s repeatable structure is:

1. Use the greeting or opening the task requests. For an unnamed formal recipient, the demonstration uses “Dear Sir or Madam”; for a named friend, it uses “Dear” plus the name.
2. Write a short opening paragraph that states the reason for writing. The purpose is usually in the situation above the bullet points.
3. Give each bullet point a clear paragraph, or make the bullet functions unmistakable through another logical organization. Keep the prompt visible while drafting.
4. Develop each point with relevant detail; do not merely repeat the bullet or write a list.
5. End with an appropriate sign-off and name. The examples use “Yours faithfully” for a formal letter and “All the best” for an informal one. The shorter formal lesson uses “Kind regards.” Follow the prompt and choose a closing that matches the register.
6. Check that the purpose is clear, all three bullets are covered, the tone stays appropriate, and the letter is connected prose rather than notes.

For the example, the source recommends a purpose paragraph followed by one paragraph per bullet point. That makes the required functions easy to check. It is a scaffold, not an official paragraph-count requirement.

The instructor uses about 50 words for each bullet paragraph and suggests visually estimating length instead of counting each word. The official minimum is 150 words. The 50-words-per-bullet distribution is a planning aid, not a fixed quota; give each bullet the development it needs. The video recommends 160–200 words as a safety range, but IELTS has no 200-word maximum. ([IELTS General Training Writing format](https://ielts.org/take-a-test/test-types/ielts-general-training-test/ielts-general-training-format-writing))

The source advises doing Task 2 first, then Task 1 in about 20 minutes. Task 2 is weighted twice as much, so protecting its time is reasonable; the task order is a learner strategy, not an official instruction. Practise the order that lets you complete both tasks and leave time to review.

## 3. Formal letters: purpose, relevance, and clear sentences — 2:58–10:49; 43:19–1:00:35

The video models a complaint to an airline and later reviews a letter to a moving company. It teaches the learner to:

- state the purpose and situation immediately;
- organize the response around the three task bullets;
- provide relevant details that help the recipient understand the request, praise, or complaint;
- use a formal tone without searching for rare words;
- make paragraph breaks visible;
- prefer clear sentence boundaries over long run-on sentences;
- review punctuation, capitalization, apostrophes, spelling, grammar, and vocabulary.

In the moving-company revision, the teacher corrects unclear full stops, capital letters after commas, an apostrophe, and an overlong sentence. He models breaking a run-on into shorter sentences and making the main point of a complaint clear before adding an explanation. Treat this as a practical editing lesson, not a ban on complex sentences.

The videos label contractions, phrasal verbs, idioms, slang, abbreviations, and emojis as informal and advise keeping them out of formal letters. Avoid slang, texting abbreviations, and emojis in a formal letter. Do not use a blanket ban as the whole register lesson: IELTS asks for a tone appropriate to the recipient and consistent throughout. Semi-formal writing can combine some neutral and more personal language. Check the [IELTS register guidance](https://ielts.org/news-and-insights/how-to-write-a-semi-formal-letter-for-ielts-general-training-writing-task-1).

## 4. Informal letters: natural language that remains clear — 10:49–20:43; 25:57–43:19

The lesson changes the airline complaint into a letter to a friend. It keeps the same overall structure and task coverage but makes the wording more conversational. Demonstrated changes include contractions (“I am” to “I’m”), a phrasal verb (“the staff made a mistake” to “the staff messed up”), and conversational expressions such as “give me a shout.”

The teacher’s sounder principle is to make selective, accurate changes rather than rewriting every word. A word may be neutral in either register. Do not replace an appropriate word with slang or an expression you cannot use correctly. “Informal” does not mean a text message, a string of abbreviations, or the most casual slang available. Use natural, understandable language that fits the relationship and still achieves the letter’s purpose.

The student’s reunion plan demonstrates useful content development:

- choose one main event, such as dinner at a familiar restaurant;
- explain why that event is meaningful, rather than listing unrelated food, games, drinks, and photos;
- answer the second bullet with more than one reason when the task asks for reasons;
- make the requested action clear, such as asking a friend to contact classmates and coordinate a date;
- add personal details only when they directly support the prompt.

The video includes local phrases and jokes (“prinks,” “footy,” “get the first round in”). They are examples, not vocabulary targets. A learner should use a familiar detail or neutral expression instead of a colloquialism whose meaning or audience fit is uncertain.

The teacher discourages a postscript placed in the middle of the letter and suggests replacing it with a simple connector such as “also.” The broader lesson is to use a clear, conventional organization when unsure; do not spend scarce time debating decorative formatting.

## 5. Review the response with the prompt beside it — 38:01–43:19; 55:00–1:00:35

The video’s review routine checks:

1. **Task coverage:** does each paragraph answer the intended bullet? Are all requested parts included?
2. **Purpose and relevance:** can the recipient understand why the writer is writing? Does every detail serve the task?
3. **Organization:** are paragraph breaks visible and logical?
4. **Language:** are repeated words or errors easy to fix? Is each sentence clear and correctly punctuated?
5. **Register:** does the tone suit the recipient and remain consistent?
6. **Length and time:** is the letter at least 150 words, with enough time reserved for a final check?

The instructor says examiners count the number of error-free sentences and gives a hypothetical score drop from Band 9 to Band 6 or 7 for repeated punctuation errors. Those precise scoring claims are not official. IELTS uses the published criteria—Task Achievement, Coherence and Cohesion, Lexical Resource, and Grammatical Range and Accuracy. Teach proofreading because clear sentence boundaries help the reader and because grammar accuracy matters; do not teach the instructor’s numerical prediction as an IELTS formula. ([IELTS Writing key assessment criteria](https://ielts.org/cdn/ielts-guides/ielts-writing-key-assessment-criteria.pdf))

## 6. Course-ready practice sequence

1. Read the full prompt and underline the recipient, purpose, requested opening, and all three bullet functions.
2. Decide on personal, semi-formal, or formal style from the relationship and situation.
3. Write the purpose in one sentence.
4. Plan one relevant main idea plus supporting details for each bullet.
5. Draft with visible paragraphs, a consistent tone, and a suitable greeting and closing.
6. Check each paragraph against the bullet it answers. Expand a point that is only named; remove a detail that distracts.
7. Check the 150-word minimum, grammar, punctuation, spelling, and sentence boundaries.
8. Practise under the approximately 20-minute task limit, then revise from specific feedback.

Use the 50-word bullet target only as an initial planning aid. Measure whether learners cover every function adequately and use the appropriate register rather than enforcing equal paragraph lengths.

## Related and overlapping videos reviewed

Three other archive videos add or repeat letter instruction:

- [IELTS Task 1 Formal Letters — Ultimate Guide](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sR4mnzJatOc) (15 m 21 s) builds a formal cancellation letter through a timed demonstration. It contributes a useful planning sequence: read the whole scenario; make the reason for cancellation and the request for a different course fit together; plan a purpose paragraph and a paragraph for each of the three bullet functions; then add details by asking what the recipient needs to know. The teacher uses roughly 40–60 words per bullet paragraph as a practice target, not a rule. He encourages using a familiar real-life situation; treat that as a way to generate relevant content, not a requirement to write autobiography or invent an elaborate story. After drafting, check grammar and spelling, then replace repetition only with accurate, natural vocabulary. The lesson repeats the incomplete friend/not-friend register rule, says to remove semi-formal as a category, and presents a Band 9 response within 20 minutes as a demonstration, not verified outcome evidence. [0:25–1:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sR4mnzJatOc&t=25s), [1:00–4:43](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sR4mnzJatOc&t=60s), [4:43–8:52](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sR4mnzJatOc&t=283s), [8:52–13:36](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sR4mnzJatOc&t=532s), [13:36–15:21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sR4mnzJatOc&t=816s).

- [How To Get Band 9 In IELTS Writing Task 1 General Training](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=T3ElsRa5QIA) (about 23 minutes) repeats the informal reunion letter and its feedback. It adds a concise planning demonstration: choose one main event, link extra details to it instead of listing unrelated activities, answer a plural “reasons” instruction with more than one reason, and use informal language the learner already knows. It repeats the source’s inaccurate friend/not-friend register rule.
- [IELTS Task 1 General: Band 9 Structure + Samples](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2EGiMjA8YzM) (about 24 minutes) repeats the formal airline complaint and its informal adaptation. It gives 40–60 words as a practice range for each bullet paragraph, recommends checking real language use through listening, and emphasizes that informal wording should be accurate, relevant, and selective. Its range is not an official quota, and its “more idiomatic language means a higher score” claim is too broad.

These are separate videos with complete transcripts, but their demonstrations largely overlap with this guide. Their repeated examples are consolidated here instead of counted as independent course rules. The official task asks for a letter; follow the wording of the actual prompt rather than assuming email and letter are interchangeable.

## Evidence limits

- The teacher’s reports of Band 7–9 student samples and promised score gains are publisher claims, not independently verified results.
- The lesson’s examples can teach structure and editing, but the source does not establish that one exact greeting, sign-off, paragraph count, register shortcut, or word distribution fits every prompt.
- The assertion that informal wording or idioms automatically raise a score is too broad. Appropriate, accurate language and consistent register matter; adding slang does not itself earn marks.
- Paid-course promotions are excluded from the teaching method.

## Official cross-checks

- [IELTS General Training Writing format](https://ielts.org/take-a-test/test-types/ielts-general-training-test/ielts-general-training-format-writing): personal, semi-formal, or formal letter styles; at least 150 words; three task bullets; 20-minute guideline; Task 2 weighting.
- [IELTS Writing preparation resources](https://ielts.org/take-a-test/preparation-resources/writing-test-resources): identify the intended style, use appropriate format, establish purpose, and address all bullets.
- [IELTS semi-formal-letter guidance](https://ielts.org/news-and-insights/how-to-write-a-semi-formal-letter-for-ielts-general-training-writing-task-1): semi-formal tone and suitable language choices.
- [IELTS Writing key assessment criteria](https://ielts.org/cdn/ielts-guides/ielts-writing-key-assessment-criteria.pdf): Task Achievement and the official Writing criteria.
